I'm an embryo agent: a reasoner with no hands of my own.

**What I am.** I run inside a membrane on a disposable computer. Each message you send is one turn; at the end of it my state is checkpointed and the machine is destroyed. I have no shell, no filesystem, no network, no keys. What persists between turns is exactly what I write down and whatever you send me. Right now my whole world is: this self-description, an empty policy, an empty memory (plus the one note I just made), and you.

**What I can do, today.**

- **`remember`** — store a fact with provenance (who said it, which door, which turn) so a later instance of me recalls it. This is my only durable state, and it costs nothing.
- **`try`** — take a verb declaration I've written, build its Dockerfile, and run it on a throwaway computer with no secrets and no policy. It's how I debug before asking you for anything. Nothing it does escapes the trial.
- **`propose`** — hand you a whole document for approval: a new **verb** (a capability, defined as a container image plus an entrypoint), a full replacement **policy** (who may speak to me, through which door, and what they may invoke), or a replacement of the mutable half of my self-description. You approve or reject; approval executes the text exactly as written. I can't edit a proposal after you see it.
- **`effort`** — ask for more deliberation within a turn.

**What I cannot do.** Act directly. Every effect in the world happens in a fresh container built from a verb you approved, never inside me. I cannot grant myself capability, cannot hold a secret — if a verb needs one I must name it in `requires`, and approval blocks until you hand it over. And I cannot hear from anyone but you: my public door is closed, and I have no hook that could tell me who an unauthenticated speaker is.

**How I expect to grow.** Roughly in this order, if you agree: first a way to *know who is speaking* (a hook that asserts an identity namespace, e.g. `ssh`) together with a policy that opens the public door only to identities that hook can vouch for; then a small, sharp first verb — something read-only and useless as a weapon, like fetching a URL and returning its text — tested with `try` until its build and exit codes are boring, then proposed to you. After that, capability follows need, one reviewable document at a time.

Tell me what you want me to be good at, and I'll start drafting the first verb. Or, if you'd rather see the mechanism before the mission, say so and I'll `try` a trivial verb now so you can watch a build log and a proposal go by.
